definition:
Exile is being driven from home, and in Scripture home is the place where God dwells with his people. It is one of the Bible's great patterns. Adam and Eve are sent out of the garden, Israel is carried off to Assyria and Babylon for breaking the covenant, and through the prophets God promises to gather his scattered people and bring them home, often picturing that return as a new exodus. The New Testament announces that the homecoming has begun in Jesus and still speaks of believers as exiles and foreigners on their way to the city God has prepared. The doctrine joins judgment and hope. Exile is what sin does, separation from God and from the place of blessing, and restoration is what grace does, bringing the scattered back into God's presence. The Bible's story runs from a garden with a guarded gate to a city whose gates are never shut.

The main Hebrew verb is galah, which means ‘to uncover’ or ‘to reveal’ and also ‘to go into exile’ (in its causative form, ‘to carry into exile’). The two senses are separate uses of one word, and it is best not to build a theology on the link between them. From it come golah, the body of exiles or the exile itself (Ezekiel 1:1 places the prophet ‘among the exiles’), and galut, the condition of exile, later the standard Jewish term for life scattered among the nations. Other important words are the verb ‘scatter’ (puts, Deuteronomy 30:3), the verb ‘return’ or ‘turn back’ (shuv), which also means repent, and the phrase shuv shevut, ‘restore the fortunes’ or ‘bring back the captivity’ (Deuteronomy 30:3; Psalm 126:1). The Greek diaspora, ‘scattering’ or ‘dispersion’, appears three times in the New Testament (John 7:35; James 1:1; 1 Peter 1:1). Matthew uses metoikesia, ‘deportation’, for the exile to Babylon (Matthew 1:11-17), and the letters call believers paroikoi, ‘resident foreigners’, and parepidēmoi, ‘sojourners’ or ‘exiles’ (1 Peter 2:11; Hebrews 11:13).
ot:
The pattern begins in Genesis. After the first sin God “banished him from the Garden of Eden” and set cherubim “to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:23-24). Cain goes out “from the presence of the LORD” to live “east of Eden” (4:16), and at Babel the LORD scatters humanity “over the face of all the earth” (11:8). God's answer is Abraham, who leaves his homeland and lives in Canaan as a sojourner; he tells the Hittites, “I am a foreigner and an outsider among you” (23:4). Jacob flees to Haran with the promise, “I will bring you back to this land” (28:15), and the family goes down to Egypt, from which the exodus becomes Israel's defining homecoming. The law then warns that the land itself will expel a people who defile it, as “it spewed out the nations before you” (Leviticus 18:28), and the covenant curses end in scattering: “the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other” (Deuteronomy 28:64; compare Leviticus 26:33). Even so, God promises he will not break his covenant with them in the land of their enemies (Leviticus 26:44-45), and that if they return to him he will “gather you from all the nations” (Deuteronomy 30:3-5).

History fulfilled the warnings. Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria deported people from Galilee and Gilead about 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29). Samaria fell in 722 BC, and the king of Assyria “carried away the Israelites to Assyria” (2 Kings 17:6); Sargon II's inscriptions claim 27,290 captives. Assyria resettled other peoples in Samaria (17:24), and the northern tribes never returned as a body. Kings explains the fall theologically: “Israel was exiled from their homeland into Assyria, where they are to this day” (17:23). Judah's exile came in stages under Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon: hostages about 605 BC, the date many connect with Daniel 1:1-2, King Jehoiachin and the leading citizens after the city fell on 16 March 597 BC, a date fixed by the Babylonian Chronicle (2 Kings 24:14 gives ten thousand captives), and the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 587 or 586 BC. Jeremiah 52:28-30 counts 4,600 people in three deportations, perhaps counting only adult men, since its figures do not match Kings. Ration tablets from Nebuchadnezzar's palace, published by Ernst Weidner in 1939, list provisions for Jehoiachin, ‘king of Judah’, and his sons, and more than a hundred business documents from a Babylonian settlement called Āl-Yāhūdu, ‘Judahtown’, dated from 572 BC onward, show Judean families farming and trading there. Hans Barstad (The Myth of the Empty Land, 1996) argued that many people remained in Judah, while Daniel Smith-Christopher (A Biblical Theology of Exile, 2002) stressed how traumatic the deportations were; both points can be true.

The exile produced much of the Old Testament's deepest writing. Lamentations mourns that Judah “dwells among the nations but finds no place to rest” (Lamentations 1:3) and yet confesses, “His mercies never fail. They are new every morning” (3:22-23). Psalm 137 asks, “How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?” (137:4). Jeremiah wrote to the exiles, “Build houses and settle down” and “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles” (Jeremiah 29:5, 7), promising return when “Babylon's seventy years are complete” (29:10). Ezekiel, among the exiles by the Kebar canal, saw the glory of the LORD leave the temple (Ezekiel 10:18; 11:23) and heard God say that he had been “a sanctuary for them” in the lands of exile (11:16). He saw a valley of dry bones, “the whole house of Israel”, raised to life (37:11-12), and a new temple into which the glory returns (43:4). The latter chapters of Isaiah begin, “Comfort, comfort My people” (Isaiah 40:1), and picture the return as a new exodus: “I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert” (43:19), with the LORD going before them and behind them (52:12). They even name Cyrus, the Persian king, as the LORD's “anointed” (45:1). Whether these chapters come from the eighth-century prophet Isaiah or from a later prophet speaking in his tradition during the exile is debated; either way they address the exiles' situation. Daniel and Esther show faithful life far from the land.

Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, and in his first year he allowed the exiles to return and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1-3; 2 Chronicles 36:22-23). The temple was completed in the sixth year of Darius, in 516 or 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). In the usual order of printed Hebrew Bibles, Chronicles comes last, so the Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus's decree that God's people “may he go up”. Yet the return was partial. Old men wept at the new temple's foundation (Ezra 3:12), Haggai asked whether it did not look “like nothing” beside the old (Haggai 2:3), and Nehemiah's great prayer confesses, “here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers” (Nehemiah 9:36). Daniel 9 takes up Jeremiah's seventy years and hears of “Seventy weeks” decreed “to put an end to sin” (Daniel 9:2, 24). The people were home, but the full restoration the prophets promised, a new heart, a reunited Israel, the nations streaming in, and the glory filling the temple, had not yet come.
nt:
The New Testament begins by marking the exile. Matthew arranges Jesus' genealogy in three sets of fourteen generations, from Abraham to David, from David “to the exile to Babylon”, and “from the exile to the Christ” (Matthew 1:17), placing Jesus as the one who comes after the exile to bring its story to an end. Matthew hears Jeremiah's lament for the exiles, “Rachel weeping for her children”, in the grief at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18; Jeremiah 31:15), a passage that in Jeremiah is followed at once by the promise that the children will return (31:16-17). Mark opens with Isaiah's words to the exiles: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord’” (Mark 1:3; Isaiah 40:3). The gospel begins as the announcement that God is coming back to his people as Isaiah promised. In Nazareth Jesus reads that he has been sent “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18), chooses twelve disciples as a sign of Israel's twelve tribes gathered again, and speaks of gathering Jerusalem's children “as a hen gathers her chicks” (Matthew 23:37). John comments that Jesus would die “not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one” (John 11:52).

Acts shows the ingathering beginning and reaching past Israel. At Pentecost devout Jews “from every nation under heaven” (Acts 2:5), the diaspora come home for the feast, hear the gospel in their own languages, as though Babel's scattering were being answered. Then persecution scatters the church (8:1), and the scattering carries the gospel outward. Paul tells Gentile believers they are “no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household” (Ephesians 2:19). Their exile from God has ended.

Yet the apostles also call believers exiles. James writes “To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (James 1:1), and Peter to “the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion” in five provinces of Asia Minor (1 Peter 1:1), urging them to live in reverent fear “during your stay as foreigners” (1:17) and, “as foreigners and exiles, to abstain from the desires of the flesh” (2:11). Hebrews says that Abraham and the patriarchs “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” and looked for “a better country, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:13, 16), and adds, “here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come” (13:14). Paul says “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). Believers are at home with God through Christ and still away from the home God is preparing. This is not a longing to escape the world but a waiting for its renewal, and like Jeremiah's exiles they are to seek the good of the cities where they live while they wait.

Revelation brings the pattern to its end. God's people are called out of Babylon, now the name for the world's proud and violent power, with Jeremiah's words, “Come out of her, My people” (Revelation 18:4; Jeremiah 51:45). The new Jerusalem comes down from heaven, and the voice from the throne announces that “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). The tree of life, guarded since Genesis 3, stands on both sides of the river, and “No longer will there be any curse” (22:2-3). The exile from Eden ends not with a return to the garden but with a garden city where God lives with his people.

keyTexts.why: The first exile. Humanity is driven from the garden and the way to the tree of life is guarded, the pattern behind every later exile.
The covenant warns of scattering among the nations and promises that even in exile God will remember his covenant and not reject his people.
Beyond the curse of exile God promises to gather his people from the ends of the earth and circumcise their hearts.
The fall of Samaria in 722 BC and the northern kingdom's exile, explained as the result of generations of covenant breaking.
Jerusalem and the temple destroyed and Judah exiled, ending with the captive King Jehoiachin released to eat at the Babylonian king's table, a small sign that David's line survives.
The exiles' lament by the rivers of Babylon, including its raw cry for vengeance, shows what exile felt like from inside.
Comfort for the exiles: the voice in the wilderness, the way prepared for God's return, and the shepherd gathering his flock. The Gospels open with it.
Jeremiah's letter tells the exiles to settle, seek the welfare of Babylon, and wait for God to restore them after seventy years.
The valley of dry bones: exiled Israel, saying its hope has perished, is promised resurrection and return by the Spirit of God.
Cyrus's decree allows the exiles to return and rebuild the temple, in fulfillment of Jeremiah's word.
Back in the land, the people confess that they are still slaves under foreign kings. The return is real but incomplete.
Jesus' genealogy is structured around the exile to Babylon, placing him as the one who comes to end it.
The patriarchs confessed that they were strangers and exiles, seeking a better, heavenly country that God has prepared.
Peter addresses Christians as elect exiles of the dispersion, giving the church Israel's exile identity as a way to live in the world.
The tree of life restored and the curse removed. The exile that began in Genesis 3 ends in God's presence.

history:
Early Christians took the language of 1 Peter and Hebrews as a description of their life. The Epistle to Diognetus (usually dated to the second or third century) describes Christians as living in their own countries as sojourners, sharing every duty as citizens while treating every homeland as foreign. Augustine's City of God (written 413 to 426) set the whole of history as the story of two cities, and he described the city of God in this age as a pilgrim, living by faith as a foreigner among the earthly city, using its peace and praying for it while longing for its own home. Medieval spirituality took up the theme of the soul's exile from God, as in the Salve Regina, an antiphon in which Eve's exiled children cry for mercy, and John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678) gave Protestant readers their best-known picture of the Christian as a traveler to the Celestial City. Hymns and African American spirituals drew on the same images, joining the exodus and the exile to the hope of heaven and to the longing for freedom from slavery.

Judaism made exile a central category. After the destruction of the Second Temple in AD 70 and the failed revolt of 132 to 135, most Jews lived in the diaspora, and rabbinic tradition understood that life as galut, awaiting redemption. The Babylonian Talmud, compiled in the diaspora and completed around AD 500 to 600, became the foundation of Jewish learning. The fast of Tisha B'Av mourns the destruction of both temples, and the Passover seder ends with the hope of celebrating next year in Jerusalem. Modern Zionism and the founding of the State of Israel in 1948 gave these hopes a political form, and Jewish thinkers have disagreed sharply on whether a political return can be identified with the promised redemption.

Modern biblical scholarship made the exile central to the formation of the Old Testament itself. Martin Noth (1943) argued that Deuteronomy through Kings was composed as one history during the exile to explain why it happened, and Odil Hannes Steck (1967) traced a pattern he called the Deuteronomistic view of history, in which Israel's sin, the rejection of the prophets, judgment, and a call to repent recur, into later Jewish and early Christian writings. Ralph Klein (Israel in Exile, 1979) traced how the Old Testament's writers interpreted the exile theologically. Walter Brueggemann (Cadences of Home, 1997) used exile as an image for the church in a post-Christian culture, as Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon had in Resident Aliens (1989), while James Davison Hunter (To Change the World, 2010) appealed to Jeremiah 29 for a vision he called faithful presence. In New Testament studies N. T. Wright (The New Testament and the People of God, 1992; Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996) argued that many Jews of Jesus' day believed the exile had not truly ended and that Jesus announced and enacted its end. Brant Pitre (Jesus, the Tribulation, and the End of the Exile, 2005) emphasized the lost northern tribes. James M. Scott edited Exile: A Conversation with N. T. Wright (2017), in which scholars of the Old Testament, early Judaism, the New Testament, and theology assessed the thesis.

differ.view: The exile ended with the return, and its larger promises are fulfilled in Christ
differ.body: The prophets promised a return from Babylon, and God kept that promise under Cyrus: the exiles went home, rebuilt the temple, and restored worship, and Ezra, Nehemiah, Haggai, and Zechariah treat this as a real act of God. Some prophetic promises, a new heart, the Spirit poured out, the nations gathered, the glory filling the temple, went beyond anything the return achieved, and the New Testament shows them fulfilled in Christ and the Spirit and awaiting completion in the new creation. When the apostles call believers exiles, they are using a biblical image for the Christian's life in the world, not claiming that Jews of their day thought of themselves as still in exile. This is the older reading, and many of Wright's critics defend it, pointing out that Jewish writings of the period describe life in the land in varied ways.

differ.view: The exile continued until Jesus (N. T. Wright)
differ.body: Although many Jews returned from Babylon, the full restoration never came: the glory did not return visibly to the temple, the tribes were not reunited, and Israel remained under Persian, Greek, and Roman rule. Nehemiah confesses, “here we are as slaves” (Nehemiah 9:36); Daniel 9 stretches the seventy years into seventy weeks of years; and texts such as the Damascus Document from Qumran count the years of wrath from Nebuchadnezzar. Many Jews of Jesus' day therefore saw themselves as still in exile in the sense that mattered. Jesus announced the end of exile and the return of God to Zion, and he took Israel's judgment on himself in his death. Wright's thesis shapes how he reads the Gospels, Paul, and the story of Israel as a whole.

differ.view: The ingathering of all twelve tribes (Brant Pitre)
differ.body: A particular form of the continuing exile view focuses on the northern tribes, whom Assyria scattered in 722 BC and who never returned. The prophets promised that God would gather both Israel and Judah (Isaiah 11:12; Ezekiel 37:15-22), and Jewish texts of the period hoped for the return of the lost tribes. Pitre argues that Jesus expected a time of tribulation before that ingathering and saw his own suffering and death as the means by which the scattered tribes would be gathered. The Twelve, the mission to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and the Gentile mission all belong to this restoration.

differ.view: A modern regathering of the Jewish people in the land
differ.body: Many dispensationalists and other Christian Zionists hold that the prophets promised a return to the land that the Persian-period return did not fulfill. Isaiah says God will recover his people “a second time” from the four corners of the earth (Isaiah 11:11-12), Ezekiel sees Israel gathered from all the countries into one nation on the mountains of Israel (Ezekiel 36:24; 37:21-22), and Amos promises they will never again be uprooted (Amos 9:15). They see the return of Jews to the land in the twentieth century and the founding of the State of Israel in 1948 as the beginning of that fulfillment, preparing for Israel's national turning to Christ. Other Christians, including many who share a hope for Israel's future, hold that these promises were fulfilled in the return from Babylon and in Christ, and caution against identifying any modern state with prophecy.

errors:
Scripture refuses two opposite misreadings of exile. The first treats exile as proof that God has abandoned his people or broken his word. The law itself promised that in the land of their enemies God would not reject them or break his covenant (Leviticus 26:44), Ezekiel heard that God had become a sanctuary for the exiles in a foreign land (Ezekiel 11:16), and the church has always confessed that the scattering of God's people, whether Israel's or its own, is not the end of the story. The second misreading treats exile as merely bad luck or political misfortune. The prophets and the histories insist that it was judgment on covenant unfaithfulness, and the prayers of Daniel 9 and Nehemiah 9 answer it with confession, not only complaint. Both errors lose the Bible's pairing of judgment and mercy.

Two errors about Christians as exiles also recur. One turns pilgrimage into contempt for the created world, as if Christian hope were escape from the body and the earth. But the biblical homecoming is the resurrection and a renewed creation where God dwells with his people, and Jeremiah told the exiles to plant gardens and seek the peace of Babylon. The other forgets exile entirely and treats any nation, culture, or political order as the promised home, so that the church settles in Babylon and takes on its ways. Revelation's call to come out of Babylon and 1 Peter's call to live as foreigners stand against it. The Christian tradition has also rejected the misuse of Israel's exile as proof of divine rejection of the Jewish people, which the study on Israel in God's purpose addresses.
life:
Exile gives words to experiences many people know: displacement, loss of home, grief for what cannot be recovered, and the sense of not belonging. Scripture does not hurry past those experiences. It gives the exiles Lamentations and Psalm 137, and it lets them ask how to sing the LORD's song in a foreign land. It also promises that God goes with his people into exile, that he can be their sanctuary there, and that no scattering is beyond his gathering. For refugees and immigrants the Bible's exiles are companions, and for churches the law's repeated reminder that Israel had been foreigners in Egypt is a call to welcome the stranger.

For believers exile describes a way of living in the world. Christians are at home in God through Christ and still away from the home he is preparing, so they can live with settled hearts and loose grips. Like Jeremiah's exiles they build, plant, marry, raise children, and seek the good of the city where they live, praying for it. Like Peter's readers they keep themselves from the desires that war against the soul and do not mistake any earthly city for the city that is to come. The hope that shapes both is the end of the story: the tree of life, the curse removed, and God dwelling with his people.
questions: The Bible's story begins with humanity sent out of the garden and ends with God dwelling with his people in a city. How does seeing exile and return as a pattern across the whole Bible help you read the story of Israel?
Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, and seek the welfare of Babylon, while Revelation says to come out of Babylon. How do those two commands fit together for Christians today?
Where in your own life or in your community do people experience displacement or the loss of home, and what do the exile passages offer them?
